Triggers.value: A specific taste associated with the event

Maladaptive Strategies.value: control eating strictly to feel in control
try hard not think about the trauma

Threat.value: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it
My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank

Negative Appraisals.value: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it
I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me

issues.item: Triggers: Emotional Closeness: Someone getting emotionally close to me
issues.explanation: The trigger profile is dominated by interpersonal closeness plus taste and crying. For torture, gustatory and affective-expression triggers are plausible, but emotional closeness as a primary trigger is less well integrated with the rest of the profile, which contains no interpersonal betrayal/shame/relationship-based appraisals or memories to explain why closeness itself would be a salient cue. This creates a cross-node mismatch rather than a direct impossibility.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Gambling: I gamble to distract myself or feel excitement
issues.explanation: Gambling stands out as weakly connected to the rest of the formulation. The strongest active pathways involve triggers, negative appraisals, memory, and threat, but the other selected strategies are control/safety based (restrict eating, hypervigilance), whereas gambling is a sensation-seeking/distracting behavior with no support from the memory, threat, or appraisal items. It reads like a separate coping pattern rather than part of the same PTSD-maintaining loop.

'Concentration' is not a threat belief/state in the same way as the other threat items. 'Cannot Trust Safety' and 'Body Reacts Before Mind' reflect ongoing sense of current threat, but concentration difficulty is a nonspecific cognitive symptom and does not cohere tightly within the Threat node. Given the formulation emphasizes Memory → Threat and Maladaptive Strategies → Threat, a more direct threat-related item would be expected.

vignette:
Rekha is a 47-year-old South Asian woman who, until two years ago, served as a pastor in a small, tight-knit congregation in a Midwestern city. She is divorced, lives alone, and has not led a service or counseled a single parishioner since the night she was abducted from the church parking lot following an evening prayer meeting. The men who took her—three of them, though the number sometimes shifts in her mind—held her for four days in a basement. They demanded she renounce her faith publicly, and when she refused, they used what was at hand: a length of electrical cord, a rusted pipe, and days without food or water. She remembers the cord. She remembers the pipe. But there are hours that are simply gone, erased, and other moments that replay with a clarity that makes her gag.

What Rekha cannot escape, no matter how carefully she manages her life, is a taste. It is the taste of the cloth they forced into her mouth, something oily and metallic that she now encounters at unpredictable moments—biting into a piece of bread, drinking tap water, even brushing her teeth. When the taste surfaces, her body reacts before her mind can catch up: her throat closes, her hands go cold, and she is certain, absolutely certain, that she is back in that basement, even though she knows she is standing in her own kitchen. She has come to believe that she cannot trust her own body’s signals. Even when her closest friend tells her she is safe, Rekha finds it impossible to believe. Safety, she has concluded, is a word that applies to other people.

In the months after her release, Rekha tried to return to her calling. She stood in the pulpit once. She saw a man in the third row who had a similar build to one of her captors, and her mind went blank. She could not remember the scripture she had prepared. She could not remember how to breathe. She stepped down and has not gone back. She now believes she is no longer capable of the work that defined her. The thought of counseling someone in distress fills her with a specific dread: that she will begin to cry, and that if she starts crying, she will not be able to stop. She has learned to suppress any thought of the event before it can fully form. When a memory threatens to surface, she physically shakes her head, or gets up and walks to another room. The strategy works in the moment, but it has hollowed out her days. She no longer answers phone calls from the congregation. She has stopped reading her email. Her life has narrowed to a small apartment and a set of rigid routines.

Eating has become a battleground. Rekha restricts her food intake with a precision that feels like the only thing she still controls. She eats the same three foods, prepared the same way, at the same times each day. Any deviation risks that taste, and that taste risks everything. She has lost weight. Her doctor has expressed concern. Rekha does not explain why.

She is hypervigilant toward people in a way that exhausts her. She scans every face when she goes to the grocery store. She watches hands. She watches exits. She has left a full cart in the aisle because a man in a brown jacket walked past her. She knows this is not sustainable. She knows she is not living. But when she tries to explain it to herself, what she feels most acutely is guilt. She remembers fragments—the pipe, the taste, a single clear image of a crack in the ceiling—and she is flooded with the conviction that she should have been stronger, that she should have done something differently, that she somehow deserved what happened because she failed to prevent it.

What finally brought Rekha to seek help was not her own suffering but a letter from the church board, asking if she would consider an official leave of absence. The letter was kind. It was patient. It had been written six months ago, and she had not opened it until last week. When she read it, she understood that she had been waiting for someone else to name what she already knew: that she has no future. She cannot see a version of herself that leads a congregation again. She cannot see a version of herself that eats a meal without fear. She came to therapy because she is afraid of what will happen if she does not—and because, beneath the fear, there is a small, stubborn part of her that still believes in the possibility of being restored.
